Pharmacogenomics individual variation & drug interactions

Why the same drug, at the same dose, helps one patient, does nothing for a second, and harms a third — and how a single letter of DNA can decide which. This guide decodes the lecture using its own figures.

§0Individual variation · the problem

Why one dose gives two outcomes

The starting puzzle of the whole lecture — and the promise that genes can solve it.

Prescribing has always assumed a kind of average patient: pick the drug for the disease, pick the standard dose, and expect the standard result. Yet clinicians have known for millennia that people are not interchangeable. Pharmacogenomics is the modern, molecular answer to that old observation — the study of how an individual's genetic inheritance affects the body's response to drugs. Before any mechanism, hold onto the scale of the problem: genetics is not a minor tweak on drug response — genetic factors account for 20–95% of the variability between patients.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

Two patients get the identical codeine dose for the same injury. One is in agony an hour later; the other stops breathing. What single thing could explain both extremes at once?

Their CYP2D6 genotype. Codeine is a prodrug that CYP2D6 converts into morphine. A poor metaboliser makes almost no morphine — hence the agony — while an ultra-rapid metaboliser floods the blood with morphine — hence the respiratory arrest. One gene, opposite catastrophes, same dose. This is the whole lecture in miniature; we build to it in §4 and §5.

An ancient intuition, a modern science

The lecture opens with Hippocrates (460–370 BC): "It is far more important to know what person has the disease than what disease the person has." That is precisely the pharmacogenomic stance — the person, not just the diagnosis, determines the right drug and dose. What was intuition for Hippocrates is now readable in the genome.

Genes are not the only source of variation. As the deck's "factors" slide lays out, drug response is shaped by a whole ring of influences — disease state, age, gender, weight, diet, environment, and drug interactions — with the genetic factor sitting alongside them. Pharmacogenomics isolates that genetic slice, which is the largest and, crucially, the one you can read in advance.

Factors affecting individual drug response (from the deck)
FactorHow it shifts drug response
Genetic factorInherited variants in enzymes, transporters, receptors — accounts for 20–95% of variability.
Disease stateOrgan dysfunction (e.g. liver/kidney) alters clearance and target sensitivity.
AgeNeonates and the elderly metabolise and excrete differently.
Gender · weightBody composition changes volume of distribution and dosing per kg.
Diet · environmentFoods and exposures (e.g. smoking) induce or inhibit metabolising enzymes.
Drug interactionOne drug alters another's kinetics or effect — the "interactions" half of this lecture.

The consequence of ignoring all this is captured in Plate 0.1. Treat everyone the same — "One Drug Fits All" — and a population splits into optimal responders, sub-optimal responders, non-responders, and people who suffer adverse reactions. Personalised medicine instead reads each person's genetic profile and matches a gene-based drug to it, shrinking the non-responder and adverse-reaction groups.

Label Key — traditional vs personalised medicine
One Drug Fits All
A single pill given to everyone. Why it matters: the same drug produces four different outcomes because the recipients differ genetically — the problem pharmacogenomics exists to fix.
Optimal / sub-optimal / non-responders
The efficacy spread within one population. Why it matters: most of this spread is invisible until you treat — unless you can predict it from genes first.
Adverse Reactions
The minority harmed by the standard drug. Why it matters: these are the patients a pre-treatment genetic test is most valuable for avoiding.
Human Diversity → GeneMap
Sorting the population by genotype. Why it matters: it converts unpredictable variation into readable genetic profiles.
Gene-based Drug A/B/C
Different drugs matched to profiles A/B/C. Why it matters: the right drug for the right genotype turns non-responders into responders.
Reasoning · why is variability so large?

A drug's journey — absorbed, distributed, metabolised, cleared, then acting on a target — is run entirely by proteins: enzymes, transporters, receptors, channels. Every one of those proteins is coded by a gene, and genes vary between people. So variation isn't noise layered on top of drug handling; it is built into every step of it. That is why a single inherited change can dominate the outcome, and why the genetic slice of variability is so wide (20–95%).

Clinical / real-world

The "adverse reactions" figure in Plate 0.1 is not abstract. Adverse drug reactions are a major cause of hospital admissions, and a large share are dose- or genotype-related. Precision medicine's promise is to move testing before the first dose — so the person who would have been in the red "adverse" group is instead started on a drug or dose their genome can tolerate.

Memory hook · the goals

"Target · Trim · Test."

The three goals of pharmacogenomics: Target — develop precisely targeted, optimal therapy; Trim — minimise drug-related adverse events; Test — develop genetic tests that predict individual response.

R Recall — the problem & the promise
  • Pharmacogenomics — studies how an individual's genetic inheritance affects the body's response to drugs.
  • Genetic share of variability — 20 to 95 percent of patient-to-patient difference.
  • Other factors — disease, age, gender, weight, diet, environment, drug interactions.
  • One-drug-fits-all outcomes — optimal, sub-optimal, non-responders, adverse reactions.
  • Three goals — target therapy, minimise adverse events, predictive genetic tests.
§1Molecular foundation

The genetic raw material: mutations, polymorphisms, SNPs

Before genes can explain drug response, we need the vocabulary of how DNA differs.

This section is deliberately placed first: every pharmacogenomic example later — a receptor that binds differently, an enzyme that works too slowly or too fast — traces back to one of the DNA changes defined here. Get the difference between a mutation, a polymorphism and a SNP straight now, and the clinical examples in §3–§5 become variations on a theme rather than a list to memorise.

Start with the substrate. Plate 1.1 shows DNA as a double helix: two sugar-phosphate backbones holding rungs of paired nucleotide bases — adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). A change in the number or order of those bases is what we call a genetic change; whether it is a "mutation" or a "polymorphism" is simply a question of how common it is.

Label Key — DNA structure
Sugar-phosphate backbone
The two outer strands that give DNA its structure. Why it matters: it is the fixed scaffold — variation happens in the bases slotted between the strands, not the backbone.
Base pairs
A–T and C–G rungs linking the strands. Why it matters: the sequence of these pairs is the code; altering one pair is exactly what a SNP does.
Cytosine (C) / Guanine (G)
A complementary pair. Why it matters: swapping a C for a T at one position is the classic single-base change seen in the SNP examples later.
Adenine (A) / Thymine (T)
The other complementary pair. Why it matters: the A118G change in §3.1 is literally an A being replaced by a G.

Mutation vs polymorphism — a frequency line at 1%

The deck draws a clean quantitative boundary. A mutation is a base change found in less than 1% of the population; a polymorphism is a DNA sequence variation that is common (>1%). Same molecular event — different prevalence. Plate 1.2 catalogues the ways bases can be disrupted: insertion (a base added), deletion (a base removed), duplication (bases repeated) and inversion (bases reversed).

Label Key — mutation types
Normal sequence
The reference C–T–A–G. Why it matters: the baseline every variant is compared against.
Insertion
An extra base added ("G" inserted). Why it matters: can shift the reading frame downstream, changing every codon that follows.
Deletion
A base removed ("A" deleted). Why it matters: like insertion, can frameshift and abolish a functional protein — one route to a "no enzyme" allele.
Duplication
Bases repeated ("CT" doubled). Why it matters: gene duplication is exactly what makes an ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metaboliser in §4.
Inversion
A segment reversed ("TA" flipped). Why it matters: reorders the code without adding or removing bases.

Zooming to a single letter — the SNP

The most important variant for this lecture is the smallest: a Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) — a DNA sequence variation occurring when a single nucleotide in the genome is altered. Plate 1.3 shows it directly: two otherwise identical helices differ at one base pair, C–G in strand 1 becoming T–A in strand 2. Typically one allele (say C) is the predominant/major allele carried by most of the population, and the other (T) is the minor variant.

Label Key — a SNP
Helix 1 (C–G)
Carries the major/predominant allele. Why it matters: it is the "reference" version most people have.
Helix 2 (T–A)
Carries the minor variant allele. Why it matters: this is the polymorphism — present in >1% of people, and potentially the one that changes drug response.
SNP (circled position)
The single differing base pair. Why it matters: whether this one letter changes the protein decides if it is silent or clinically important (see below).

A SNP's consequence depends on whether it changes the protein. The deck splits them in two: synonymous SNPs result in the same protein, while non-synonymous SNPs result in a different protein. That single distinction is the hinge of pharmacogenetics — it predicts whether a variant is silent or functional.

Reasoning · why can a base change be silent?

The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are specified by more than one codon (e.g. both GAA and GAG code for glutamate). So a base swap that lands on the "wobble" position can produce a different codon that still codes for the same amino acid — a synonymous change, protein unchanged. A swap that changes the amino acid is non-synonymous, and only then can the protein's shape, activity or binding change. This is exactly why the ABCB1 3435C>T SNP in §4.3 (synonymous, I1145I) is expected to be silent, while the A118G SNP in §3.1 (asparagine→aspartate) is potentially functional.

Clinical / real-world

The 1% frequency line is not academic. A rare mutation may explain one striking patient (e.g. the rare VKORC1 warfarin-resistant carrier in §3.2), but a common polymorphism — carried by tens of percent of people — is what makes pharmacogenetic testing worthwhile at population scale. You test for variants common enough to catch, and consequential enough to matter.

Memory hook · silent vs meaningful

"Synonymous = Synonyms = Same meaning."

A synonym is a different word with the same meaning → a synonymous SNP is a different codon with the same amino acid → same protein. Non-synonymous = new meaning = different protein.

R Recall — mutations, polymorphisms & SNPs
  • Mutation vs polymorphism — mutation <1% of population, polymorphism >1% (common).
  • Mutation types — insertion, deletion, duplication, inversion.
  • SNP — a variation at a single altered nucleotide; one major allele + one minor variant.
  • Synonymous SNP — same amino acid → same protein (silent).
  • Non-synonymous SNP — different amino acid → different protein (potentially functional).
  • Why silent is possible — the genetic code is degenerate (redundant codons).
§2Definitions & framework

Two words, two levels

Pharmacogenomics vs pharmacogenetics — and the PK/PD scaffold that organises every example.

The lecture uses two similar terms and one organising diagram. Nail both here and the rest of the guide slots neatly into place: §3 is the pharmacodynamic branch, §4 the pharmacokinetic branch.

Pharmacogenomics vs pharmacogenetics

The word pharmacogenomics fuses pharmacology (the science of drugs) with genomics (the study of genes and their functions) — hence, the study of how genetic inheritance affects drug response, viewed genome-wide. Pharmacogenetics is a subset: the study of how inherited variation affects drug response and metabolism, but focused on the variations in a single targeted gene or a group of functionally related genes. In short — same idea, different resolution.

Pharmacogenomics vs pharmacogenetics
FeaturePharmacogenomicsPharmacogenetics
ScopeGenome-wide — many genes at onceA subset — one gene or a group of related genes
Root wordsPharmacology + genomicsPharmacology + genetics
Typical questionHow does a person's whole genetic makeup shape drug response?How does variation in this gene affect this drug?
RelationshipPharmacogenetics is a subset of pharmacogenomics.

The two levels: pharmacokinetics vs pharmacodynamics

The deck's pivotal framing slide asks: how and at what level can genetic variation affect drug response? The answer is that genetic polymorphisms act at two levels. Pharmacokinetics (PK) is "what the body does to the drug" — absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME). Pharmacodynamics (PD) is "what the drug does to the body" — its action on receptors, ion channels, transporters and enzyme targets. A variant can strike at either level, and the clinical consequence differs.

Where genetic variation strikes: PK vs PD
Pharmacokinetics (PK)Pharmacodynamics (PD)
SloganWhat the body does to the drugWhat the drug does to the body
Processes / targetsAbsorption · Distribution · Metabolism · ExcretionReceptors · Ion channels · Transporters · Enzymes (as drug targets)
Effect of a variantChanges drug exposure (concentration reaching the target)Changes drug effect at a given concentration
Lecture examplesCYP2D6, P-glycoprotein/ABCB1 (§4)µ-opioid receptor A118G, VKORC1/VKOR (§3)
Reasoning · why the PK/PD split predicts the consequence

The split isn't just tidy naming — it tells you what will go wrong. A PK variant changes how much drug reaches the target: too little metabolism → drug accumulates → toxicity; too much → drug is cleared before it works → failure. A PD variant leaves the concentration normal but changes the target's response — the drug is present but the lock has changed shape. Knowing which level a gene sits at tells you whether to reach for a dose adjustment (PK) or a different drug (PD).

Clinical / real-world

Warfarin (§3.2) is the textbook case of both levels at once: its target enzyme is a PD gene (VKORC1) and its clearance is a PK gene (CYP2C9). That is why warfarin dosing algorithms read both genotypes — a single-level view would mis-dose the patient.

Memory hook · which way round?

"Kinetics = body Kicks the drug around; Dynamics = Drug Does something."

PK — the body kicks the drug through ADME. PD — the drug does its action on the target.

R Recall — definitions & the two levels
  • Pharmacogenomics — pharmacology + genomics; genome-wide study of genes and drug response.
  • Pharmacogenetics — a subset; inherited variation in one gene or related genes.
  • Pharmacokinetics — what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
  • Pharmacodynamics — what the drug does to the body: receptors, ion channels, transporters, enzymes.
  • PK variant vs PD variant — changes drug exposure vs changes drug effect.
§3Pharmacodynamics · the target

Variation in the target

When the drug arrives at a normal concentration but the target itself is genetically different.

Pharmacodynamic variation changes the lock, not the key's delivery. Here the drug reaches its site at the expected level, but a SNP has altered the receptor or enzyme it acts on. Two examples anchor the idea: a receptor (µ-opioid, §3.1) and an enzyme drug target (VKOR/warfarin, §3.2).

§3.1At receptor level — A118G in the µ-opioid receptor

The µ-opioid receptor is the target of opioids like morphine. It carries a common SNP, A118G: an A→G substitution at nucleotide 118 that swaps asparagine (N) for aspartic acid (D) in the receptor's N-terminal domain. Plate 3.1 shows the receptor as a "snake plot" of its amino-acid chain threading seven times through the membrane, with the position 118 residue highlighted near the N-terminal tail. This variant is common — occurring in roughly 40–50% — and has been implicated in drug addiction, stress responsivity, dependence and pain reduction, although the evidence is conflicting.

Label Key — µ-opioid receptor variant
N-terminal domain
The extracellular tail where residue 118 sits. Why it matters: the N-terminus helps shape ligand access; a change here can subtly alter how opioids engage the receptor.
Highlighted residue (position 118)
Where asparagine becomes aspartic acid. Why it matters: a non-synonymous change — the amino acid, and so potentially receptor behaviour, is altered.
Seven membrane passes
The receptor is a 7-transmembrane (GPCR) protein. Why it matters: identifies it as a classic drug-target receptor whose signalling can be tuned by variants.
Reasoning · why a receptor SNP is a PD change

Absorption, metabolism and excretion of the opioid are untouched by A118G — the drug still reaches the receptor at a normal concentration. What changes is the receptor's response to that concentration. Because the variant sits in the protein the drug acts on, not in any ADME pathway, it is a pharmacodynamic variant by definition. The "conflicting evidence" caveat is itself instructive: a non-synonymous SNP can change function, but whether it changes it enough to matter clinically is a separate, harder question.

Clinical / real-world

Because A118G has been linked to differences in pain relief and dependence, it has been proposed as a marker for opioid responsiveness and addiction risk. The lecture's honesty here is the lesson: the association is real but inconsistent, so A118G is not a reliable stand-alone test the way HLA-B*5701 is for abacavir (§5). A candidate biomarker must be both functional and reproducible before it guides prescribing.

§3.2Enzyme as a target — VKORC1 & warfarin

The second PD example is an enzyme drug target. Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR) regenerates reduced vitamin K, the cofactor a carboxylase needs to convert precursor vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) into their biologically active forms. Plate 3.2 traces the cycle: precursor factors are carboxylated using reduced vitamin K, which is oxidised to the epoxide, and VKORC1 normally reduces it back. Warfarin inhibits VKOR (the red cross), breaking the cycle and reducing synthesis of active clotting factors — the basis of its anticoagulant effect.

Label Key — vitamin K cycle & warfarin
Vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X
Clotting factors needing carboxylation to work. Why it matters: these are the ultimate output warfarin suppresses to prevent clots.
Carboxylase
Activates precursor factors using reduced vitamin K. Why it matters: it consumes reduced vitamin K, creating the demand that VKOR must keep meeting.
VKORC1 (red cross)
The enzyme that recycles vitamin K epoxide back to the reduced form — the warfarin target. Why it matters: blocking it starves the carboxylase of cofactor, so anticoagulation; a resistant variant of it defeats warfarin.
S-warfarin → CYP2C9
The more potent enantiomer, cleared by CYP2C9. Why it matters: makes CYP2C9 a PK co-determinant of warfarin levels.
R-warfarin → CYP1A2 / CYP3A4
The less potent enantiomer's clearance route. Why it matters: shows warfarin handling is spread across several enzymes.

Now the genetics. VKOR is encoded by VKORC1, and a rare mutation in this gene causes warfarin resistance. Because warfarin can no longer inhibit the altered enzyme effectively, carriers require exceptionally high warfarin doses to achieve effective anticoagulation.

Reasoning · resistance, not sensitivity — why?

It is tempting to assume any VKORC1 variant makes warfarin "not work" by lowering the enzyme. The mechanism is the opposite of sensitivity: the variant VKOR still functions but is less inhibited by warfarin. So at a normal warfarin dose the enzyme keeps recycling vitamin K, clotting factors keep being made, and the patient stays coagulable. Only a much larger dose inhibits enough enzyme to anticoagulate — hence resistance. (Other VKORC1 promoter variants, not the focus here, do the reverse and increase sensitivity.)

Clinical / real-world

Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index: too little and clots form, too much and the patient bleeds. This is why it is the poster-child for pharmacogenomic dosing — response depends on the PD target gene (VKORC1) and the PK clearance gene (CYP2C9) together. Genotype-guided algorithms use both to pick a safer starting dose, shortening the dangerous trial-and-error period of INR titration.

Memory hook · which factors need vitamin K

"1972" — factors II, VII, IX, X are vitamin K-dependent.

Read as 2-7-9-10. Warfarin, by blocking VKOR, quietly turns all four off.

R Recall — pharmacodynamic variation
  • PD variation — the drug reaches its site normally but the target (receptor/enzyme) is altered.
  • A118G — µ-opioid receptor SNP; A→G at nucleotide 118, asparagine→aspartic acid in the N-terminal; ~40–50%.
  • A118G evidence — linked to addiction/pain response but conflicting (not a reliable test).
  • VKOR / warfarin — warfarin inhibits VKOR, cutting active clotting factors II, VII, IX, X.
  • VKORC1 mutation — causes warfarin resistance → needs exceptionally high doses.
  • Warfarin enantiomers — S→CYP2C9 (potent), R→CYP1A2/CYP3A4.
§4Pharmacokinetics · disposition

Variation in disposition

When the target is normal but genetics changes how much drug ever reaches it.

Pharmacokinetic variation is the larger, more clinically actionable half. Here the target works fine, but a variant enzyme or transporter changes the drug's exposure — too much (toxicity) or too little (failure), or, for prodrugs, too little active drug. The dominant players are the drug-metabolising cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes and the efflux transporter P-glycoprotein.

§4.1CYP2D6 and the metaboliser classes

Cytochrome P450 enzymes carry out much of hepatic drug metabolism. CYP2D6 is the archetype: it metabolises many clinically used medications and is highly polymorphic — over 100 variants and subvariants. Those variants sort each person into a metaboliser class, and Plate 4.4 shows how the same gene produces the full spectrum, from no enzyme to increased enzyme.

Label Key — genotype → phenotype flow
Gene deletion → no enzyme
e.g. CYP2D6*4,*5 → no metabolism. Why it matters: the molecular basis of a poor metaboliser.
Unstable enzyme → decreased metabolism
e.g. CYP2D6*10. Why it matters: underlies the intermediate metaboliser — reduced but not absent activity.
Normal enzyme → normal metabolism
e.g. CYP2D6*1. Why it matters: the reference extensive (normal) metaboliser.
Altered substrate specificity → other metabolites
e.g. CYP2C9*3. Why it matters: the enzyme works but on the "wrong" reaction — a subtler failure mode.
Gene duplication → higher enzyme levels
e.g. CYP2D6*2N → increased metabolism. Why it matters: the basis of the ultra-rapid metaboliser.

The four phenotypes and their frequencies (Caucasian) are set out in the CYP2D6 variant table from the deck:

Selected CYP2D6 variants (from the deck) — variant → function → phenotype
VariantEnzyme functionPhenotype produced
*1NormalExtensive metaboliser (EM) — the reference
*2NormalExtensive metaboliser (EM)
*3Loss of functionPoor metaboliser (PM) if two loss-of-function alleles / IM
*4Loss of functionPoor metaboliser (PM) — the most common PM allele in Caucasians (12–23%)
*5Loss of function (gene deletion)Poor metaboliser (PM)
*6Loss of functionPoor metaboliser (PM)
*9Decreased activityIntermediate metaboliser (IM)
The four CYP2D6 metaboliser phenotypes (Caucasian frequencies from the deck)
PhenotypeGenotype basisFrequencyConsequence for a normal drug
Ultra-rapid (UM)Gene duplication/multiplication5–10%Clears drug too fast → sub-therapeutic; for a prodrug, too much active drug
Extensive (EM)Two functional alleles (normal)65–80%Standard, expected handling
Intermediate (IM)Reduced-function alleles10–15%Somewhat reduced clearance
Poor (PM)Two loss-of-function alleles5–10%Drug accumulates → toxicity; for a prodrug, little/no active drug
Reasoning · why "poor" and "ultra-rapid" mean opposite things for prodrugs

The trap is to assume "poor metaboliser = weak drug effect." It depends on whether the drug is active as given or a prodrug. For an active drug (e.g. nortriptyline), a poor metaboliser clears it slowly → high levels → toxicity. For a prodrug that CYP2D6 activates (codeine → morphine; tamoxifen → endoxifen), a poor metaboliser makes too little active drug → therapy fails, while an ultra-rapid metaboliser can make dangerously much. Same enzyme, opposite clinical results depending on the direction of metabolism.

Memory hook · the four classes

"UEIP — Under, Even, Intermediate, Piled-up."

Ultra-rapid (drug runs under the therapeutic level), Extensive (even/normal), Intermediate, Poor (drug piles up). Only EM behaves as the textbook dose intends.

§4.2Seeing it in practice — nortriptyline & tamoxifen

Nortriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant metabolised by CYP2D6, and it makes the metaboliser effect visible. Plate 4.1 plots plasma concentration over time against the number of functional CYP2D6 genes (0, 1, 2, 3, 13). With 0 functional genes (poor metaboliser) the parent drug piles up to the highest levels; with 13 functional genes (ultra-rapid) it stays lowest. The active-tracking metabolite 10-hydroxynortriptyline shows the mirror image — highest in the 13-gene carrier who metabolises fastest.

Label Key — nortriptyline PK curves
Curve "0" (left, top)
Zero functional CYP2D6 genes = poor metaboliser. Why it matters: highest parent-drug levels → toxicity risk on a standard dose.
Curve "13" (left, bottom)
Thirteen gene copies = ultra-rapid metaboliser. Why it matters: lowest parent-drug levels → likely sub-therapeutic.
Right panel (10-hydroxynortriptyline)
The metabolite. Why it matters: its reversed ordering confirms the parent is being converted faster when more functional genes are present.

This directly changes dosing. As the deck's population histogram (Plate 4.2) shows, the metaboliser classes need very different nortriptyline doses — poor metabolisers need low doses (~20–50 mg/day) while ultra-rapid metabolisers need high doses (>250–500 mg/day) to reach the same exposure.

Label Key — metaboliser distribution & dose
Genotype row
Cartoon alleles (functional/reduced) per class. Why it matters: ties the visible phenotype back to the number of working genes.
Phenotype row (UM/EM/IM/PM)
The four classes across the distribution. Why it matters: most people are extensive; the tails are where dosing must change.
Frequency (Caucasian)
UM 5–10%, EM 65–80%, IM 10–15%, PM 5–10%. Why it matters: quantifies how many patients a test would reclassify.
Nortriptyline dose bar
Dose need runs from >250–500 mg (UM) to 20–50 mg (PM). Why it matters: the same target level demands an order-of-magnitude different dose across classes.
Worked example · adjusting nortriptyline dose to metaboliser class

An extensive (normal) metaboliser reaches a therapeutic plasma level on 100 mg/day of nortriptyline. Estimate a rational starting dose for (a) a poor metaboliser and (b) an ultra-rapid metaboliser, reasoning from the deck's dose-requirement bar (PM ≈ 20–50 mg/day, EM ≈ 100–150 mg/day, UM ≈ >250–500 mg/day).

  1. State the principle: at steady state, average concentration C̅ ∝ Dose / CL. Metaboliser class changes clearance CL, so to hold C̅ constant the dose must move with clearance.
  2. Poor metaboliser: clearance is much lower, so the standard dose would over-shoot. From the bar, the PM band is ~20–50 mg/day — roughly ¼ to ½ of the EM dose. Starting point: ~25–50 mg/day.
  3. Ultra-rapid metaboliser: clearance is much higher, so the standard dose under-shoots. The UM band is >250–500 mg/day — several-fold the EM dose. Starting point: ~250 mg/day and up, titrated with levels.
  4. Sanity check against Plate 4.1: the 0-gene (PM) curve sat highest and the 13-gene (UM) curve lowest on an identical dose — exactly why the PM needs less and the UM needs more.

Answer: start the poor metaboliser low (~25–50 mg/day) and the ultra-rapid metaboliser high (~250+ mg/day), then titrate to plasma level. The genotype sets the ballpark; monitoring fine-tunes it.

Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) for breast cancer, drives the point home from the opposite direction — it is a prodrug. Plate 4.3 traces its activation: CYP2D6 (with CYP3A4/5 and others) converts tamoxifen and N-desmethyltamoxifen into the potent active metabolites 4-hydroxytamoxifen and, most importantly, endoxifen. A poor CYP2D6 metaboliser generates less endoxifen — so, unlike nortriptyline, poor metabolism here means weaker anti-cancer effect, not toxicity.

Label Key — tamoxifen activation
Tamoxifen
The parent prodrug given to the patient. Why it matters: weakly active until CYP-activated — so response depends on the patient's enzymes.
CYP2D6 step
Converts intermediates to the active metabolites. Why it matters: the rate-limiting, genotype-sensitive activation — the reason CYP2D6 status predicts tamoxifen benefit.
Endoxifen (& 4-hydroxytamoxifen)
The potent active anti-oestrogen metabolites. Why it matters: these do the therapeutic work; less endoxifen = less effect.
CYP3A4/5
Performs the N-demethylation to N-desmethyltamoxifen. Why it matters: shows activation is a multi-enzyme relay, not one gene alone.
Clinical / real-world

Two CYP2D6 drugs, opposite lessons. A poor metaboliser on nortriptyline risks toxicity and needs a lower dose; a poor metaboliser on tamoxifen risks treatment failure (too little endoxifen) and gains nothing from a higher dose of a drug she cannot activate — a different drug may be needed. Same enzyme, same "poor metaboliser" label, but you must know whether the drug is active or a prodrug before you act.

§4.3Transporters — P-glycoprotein, ABCB1 and digoxin

Metabolism is not the only PK step under genetic control — drug distribution depends on transporters. The major one is P-glycoprotein (P-gp), also called MDR1 or ABCB1: a large efflux pump that moves drugs out. In the gut, liver and kidney it pumps drugs out of the body; at the brain endothelium it pumps drugs back into the blood, guarding the blood-brain barrier. Being a large protein, it carries plenty of SNPs, and polymorphisms in P-gp can affect drug responses.

The lecture's worked case is the ABCB1 3435C>T polymorphism and digoxin (used for heart conditions, and with a narrow therapeutic index). Crucially, 3435C>T is a synonymous SNP (I1145I) — the codon changes (ATC→ATT) but the amino acid, isoleucine, does not. Plate 4.5 shows the data: duodenal P-gp is lowest in the TT genotype, and plasma digoxin Cmax runs higher in TT than CC.

Label Key — ABCB1 / digoxin data
Left plot — duodenal P-gp by genotype
CC highest → CT → TT lowest. Why it matters: less gut pump in TT means less drug pumped back out into the lumen.
Right plot — plasma digoxin Cmax
Higher in TT than CC. Why it matters: the mirror of the left plot — less efflux → more absorbed → higher blood levels.
CC / CT / TT
The three genotypes at position 3435. Why it matters: shows an apparent gene-dose trend across the genotypes.
Reasoning · why a "silent" SNP shows an effect — and why to distrust it

Here is the deck's deliberate curveball. 3435C>T is synonymous (I1145I) — by the rule in §1 it should not change the P-gp protein at all, so it should be functionally silent. Yet the data look like an effect (lower TT P-gp, higher TT digoxin). The lecture's verdict: there is no strong evidence that the SNP is associated with altered P-gp levels or location. The lesson is that an observed association is not proof of a mechanism — a synonymous SNP can be a marker riding along with (in linkage with) a truly functional variant elsewhere, or the association can be a statistical artefact. Always ask whether a SNP changes the protein before believing it changes the drug.

Clinical / real-world

Digoxin's narrow therapeutic index is why even a modest shift in absorption matters — a small rise in Cmax can tip a patient toward toxicity (nausea, arrhythmia, visual changes). But because the 3435C>T evidence is weak, this SNP is not a validated dosing test — a cautionary counterpoint to the strong, actionable tests in §5.

Memory hook · P-gp's three names & its job

"P-gp = MDR1 = ABCB1 — the bouncer that pumps drugs OUT."

MDR = multi-drug resistance: tumours over-express it to eject chemo. Gut/liver/kidney → out of the body; brain endothelium → back into blood.

R Recall — pharmacokinetic variation
  • CYP2D6 — hepatic metaboliser, highly polymorphic (>100 variants).
  • Four classes — ultra-rapid, extensive, intermediate, poor (gene duplication → UM; loss-of-function → PM).
  • Poor metaboliser — active drug accumulates → toxicity; prodrug not activated → failure.
  • Nortriptyline — highest levels with 0 functional CYP2D6 genes, lowest with 13; PM needs a lower dose.
  • Tamoxifen — a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to endoxifen; poor metabolisers get less benefit.
  • P-glycoprotein — MDR1 / ABCB1, an efflux pump (out in gut/liver/kidney, into blood at brain).
  • ABCB1 3435C>T — synonymous (I1145I); TT shows higher digoxin but no strong evidence of altered P-gp.
§5Application · precision medicine

From genotype to prescription

Turning all of the above into a test done before the first dose — and knowing its limits.

Everything so far explains why individuals differ. This closing section is the payoff: using that knowledge as a genetic test to choose the drug and dose in advance. The deck frames testing around two questions — will it work, and will it be safe?

What genetic testing answers (from the deck)
GoalQuestion the test answersExample
Drug efficacyWill my cancer respond to this drug? Will the drug be activated when I take it?Codeine, tramadol (CYP2D6-activated prodrugs); tumour markers
Drug safetyWill a drug cause a life-threatening reaction? What dose will I need?Abacavir hypersensitivity; azathioprine marrow suppression

The codeine/tramadol line ties §4 to real prescribing: both are CYP2D6-activated prodrugs, so a test that reports metaboliser status predicts whether the active opioid will even be formed — precisely the scenario in this section's opening Predict beat.

Medicare-rebated tests in Australia

The deck names the two pharmacogenetic tests rebated by Medicare in Australia — the ones with strong enough evidence to be standard care:

  • HLA-B*5701 before abacavir (HIV) — carriers of this variant risk severe/deadly hypersensitivity in ~5%. Testing and avoiding abacavir in carriers essentially eliminates the reaction.
  • Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) before azathioprine (immunosuppression) — low TPMT activity risks 1–5% bone-marrow suppression, a potentially fatal drop in blood counts.

Beyond the rebated pair, broader panels are available on request. The deck lists the genes such panels test: CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, CYP2C9, VKORC1, ABCB1, OPRM1 and SLCO1B1 — a roll-call that revisits nearly every gene from this lecture (CYP2D6/CYP2C9 metabolism, VKORC1 warfarin target, ABCB1 transporter, OPRM1 µ-opioid receptor).

Reasoning · why HLA-B*5701 is rebated but A118G and 3435C>T are not

Compare the evidence quality across the lecture. HLA-B*5701 → abacavir hypersensitivity is a strong, reproducible, high-consequence association with a clear action (don't use the drug). The µ-opioid A118G (§3.1) is conflicting, and the ABCB1 3435C>T (§4.3) has no strong evidence of a functional effect. A test earns a place in routine care only when the variant is common enough to catch, functional enough to matter, and reproducible enough to trust — and when knowing it changes what you do.

Clinical / real-world · precision medicine

This is the destination the lecture has been building toward: comprehensive genetic testing to make drug use more effective and safer — precision (personalised) medicine. In practice it is arriving unevenly: a handful of tests (HLA-B*5701, TPMT, and DPYD before fluoropyrimidines) are standard, warfarin and CYP2D6 dosing are used in some centres, and many proposed markers remain research-grade. The take-home is measured optimism — real where evidence is strong, cautious where it is not.

Memory hook · the two rebated tests

"Abacavir needs Antigen (HLA); Azathioprine needs an Antidote enzyme (TPMT)."

Two A-drugs, two safety tests: HLA-B*5701 for abacavir, TPMT for azathioprine.

Take-home messages

The deck closes on three take-homes, which double as this guide's spine:

  • Pharmacogenomics and pharmacogenetics — the genome-wide science and its single-gene subset (§2).
  • Individual variation can affect drug disposition (PK) or action (PD) — the two levels (§3–§4).
  • Pharmacogenetic tests inform personalised drug therapy — the applied payoff (§5).
R Recall — testing & precision medicine
  • Testing answers two things — drug efficacy (will it work / be activated?) and drug safety (harmful reaction? what dose?).
  • Codeine & tramadol — CYP2D6-activated prodrugs; testing predicts activation.
  • HLA-B*5701 — test before abacavir; ~5% risk of severe/deadly hypersensitivity.
  • TPMT — test before azathioprine; 1–5% risk of bone-marrow suppression.
  • Panel genes — CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP1A2, CYP3A4/5, CYP2C9, VKORC1, ABCB1, OPRM1, SLCO1B1.
  • Take-home — variation affects disposition or action; tests enable personalised (precision) medicine.
